description: The theory behind statistical inference: probability foundations, optimal estimation, likelihood and Bayes methods, hypothesis testing, asymptotics, high-dimensional statistics and non-parametric methods. Students prove core results on paper and then test them with simulation studies in the maths lab and code runner.
modelledOn: Lehmann and Casella, Theory of Point Estimation
Wainwright, High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint
outcomes: Prove and apply convergence results, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem to statistical estimators.
Derive sufficient statistics, optimal unbiased estimators and information bounds for standard models.
Construct maximum likelihood and Bayes estimators, compute them numerically and compare them under a loss function.
Derive most powerful and likelihood-based tests and confidence regions, and prove their error properties.
Establish consistency and asymptotic normality of estimators, including under model misspecification.
Analyse high-dimensional and non-parametric procedures with concentration inequalities and verify claims by simulation.

units.title: Probability foundations for inference
topics: Probability spaces, random variables and expectation as an integral
Modes of convergence: almost sure, in probability, in L^p and in distribution; Slutsky's lemma
The law of large numbers and the central limit theorem via characteristic functions
Inequalities: Markov, Chebyshev, Hoeffding and Jensen
Statistical models, exponential families and identifiability

units.title: Point estimation theory
topics: Sufficiency, the factorisation theorem and minimal sufficiency
Completeness, the Rao-Blackwell theorem and the Lehmann-Scheffe theorem
Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao lower bound
Method of moments, bias-variance trade-off and mean squared error
Decision theory: loss, risk, admissibility and minimax estimators

units.title: Maximum likelihood and Bayes estimation
topics: Likelihood, score function and maximum likelihood estimators; invariance
Numerical maximisation: Newton-Raphson, Fisher scoring and the EM algorithm
Bayes estimators, conjugate priors and Bayes risk
Empirical Bayes and the James-Stein shrinkage estimator
Objective priors, Jeffreys prior and the Bernstein-von Mises theorem

units.title: Hypothesis testing and confidence regions
topics: Neyman-Pearson lemma and most powerful tests
Uniformly most powerful tests, monotone likelihood ratio and unbiased tests
Likelihood ratio, Wald and score tests; Wilks' theorem
Confidence sets, pivots and test inversion
p-values, multiple testing and false discovery rate
Bayes factors and Bayesian testing

units.title: Asymptotic theory
topics: Consistency of the maximum likelihood estimator and its asymptotic normality
The delta method and variance-stabilising transformations
M-estimators, the sandwich variance and misspecified models
Asymptotic relative efficiency and local asymptotic normality
U-statistics and the empirical distribution function: Glivenko-Cantelli theorem

units.title: High-dimensional statistics
topics: Concentration of measure: sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential variables
Sparse linear regression: the lasso, oracle inequalities and the restricted eigenvalue condition
Covariance estimation and random matrix theory (Marchenko-Pastur law)
Minimax lower bounds: Le Cam and Fano methods
Multiple testing in high dimensions; knockoffs for variable selection
Phase transitions when p exceeds n

units.title: Non-parametric methods
topics: The empirical distribution, the DKW inequality and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
Rank tests: Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis; Hodges-Lehmann estimators
Kernel density estimation: bias, variance and bandwidth selection
Non-parametric regression: local polynomials, splines and convergence rates
Permutation tests, exact inference and conformal prediction

units.title: Simulation studies and research practice
topics: Designing a Monte Carlo study to compare estimators: replications, metrics and error bars
Reading a statistical-theory paper: assumptions, main theorem, proof sketch and limits
Writing a rigorous proof and a clear technical report
Project: derive, prove and simulate the properties of an estimator for an applied problem

schedule.title: Probability tools and convergence
schedule.exercise: Prove the weak law of large numbers by Chebyshev, state Slutsky's lemma and use the central limit theorem to approximate a binomial tail probability for a sample of polling data.

tasks.title: Overlay the standardised sample mean distribution for n = 5, 30 and 200 from a skewed distribution on the normal curve and compare quantiles
Simulate convergence in probability and in distribution for a sample maximum and show with 10000 trials that they are different
Check Hoeffding's bound against simulated tail frequencies for sums of bounded variables and report how loose the bound is

schedule.title: Sufficiency and unbiased estimation
schedule.exercise: Show that the sample sum is sufficient and complete for a Poisson model, derive the minimum variance unbiased estimator of e^(-lambda) by Rao-Blackwell, and check against the Cramer-Rao bound.

tasks.title: Use the factorisation theorem to identify a sufficient statistic for three given families and write each likelihood in factored form
Compute the Fisher information and Cramer-Rao bound for the exponential rate parameter and compare with the variance of the sample mean
Simulate a crude unbiased estimator and its Rao-Blackwellised version for a Poisson probability and show the variance reduction over 5000 runs

schedule.title: Risk, shrinkage and decisions
schedule.exercise: Compare the sample mean, a shrinkage estimator and a constant for a normal mean under squared error loss, plotting risk against the true mean and discussing admissibility and minimax.

tasks.title: Compute the bias, variance and mean squared error of two variance estimators (divide by n and by n-1) and plot the MSE against sample size
Plot the risk functions of three estimators of a normal mean on a grid and identify which are dominated
Simulate the James-Stein estimator in 10 dimensions and show that its total squared error beats the sample mean for every true mean tried

schedule.title: Maximum likelihood in practice
schedule.exercise: Derive the maximum likelihood estimators for a gamma shape and rate, explain why there is no closed form, and fit them to rainfall data with Newton-Raphson and EM.

tasks.title: Derive and plot the log-likelihood of an exponential sample and mark the maximum and the Fisher information at the maximum
Implement Newton-Raphson and Fisher scoring for a Poisson regression and compare the number of iterations to converge
Fit a two-component Gaussian mixture to market-price data with the EM algorithm and show the log-likelihood rising at every iteration

schedule.title: Bayes estimators and shrinkage
schedule.exercise: Derive the posterior mean for a beta-binomial model, compare its risk with the maximum likelihood estimator under squared error, and explain empirical Bayes for clinic-level rates.

tasks.title: Compute the posterior mean and Bayes risk for a Beta prior and binomial data and compare against the MLE for small samples
Estimate the prior from 50 clinic-level counts using empirical Bayes and compare shrunken rates with raw rates in a mean squared error simulation
Compute the Jeffreys prior for a Poisson rate and check by simulation that credible intervals have near-nominal frequentist coverage as n grows

schedule.title: Most powerful tests
schedule.exercise: Use the Neyman-Pearson lemma to construct the most powerful test for a normal mean, plot its power curve and show the likelihood ratio, Wald and score tests for a binomial proportion.

tasks.title: Derive the most powerful size 0.05 test between two normal means, and plot its power as the difference between the means grows
Compute likelihood ratio, Wald and score statistics for a binomial proportion and compare their actual sizes at n = 10, 30 and 100
Find a uniformly most powerful test for an exponential rate using monotone likelihood ratio and plot its power function

schedule.title: Confidence sets, p-values and Bayes factors
schedule.exercise: Invert a family of tests to build a confidence interval, then compute p-values, adjust for 20 tests with false discovery rate control, and compare the result with a Bayes factor.

tasks.title: Check the coverage of Wald, likelihood ratio and exact binomial intervals over a grid of true proportions with 10000 simulations each
Simulate 1000 tests with 10 percent true effects, apply Bonferroni and a step-up procedure, and compare false discovery proportion and power
Compute the Bayes factor for a point null versus a normal alternative and show how it depends on the prior width

schedule.title: Asymptotics of estimators
schedule.exercise: Prove the asymptotic normality of a maximum likelihood estimator in the regular case, apply the delta method to a ratio of means, and compute the sandwich variance when the model is wrong.

tasks.title: Apply the delta method to the log odds of a proportion and compare the approximate standard error with simulation
Simulate MLEs for a Weibull shape across n = 20 to 2000 and check that the standardised error approaches a normal distribution
Fit a Poisson model to overdispersed data, compare model-based and sandwich standard errors, and show which gives correct coverage

schedule.title: Concentration and sparse regression
schedule.exercise: State the oracle inequality for the lasso, explain the role of the restricted eigenvalue condition and simulate support recovery as the number of predictors grows.

tasks.title: Plot the tail of a sub-Gaussian and a sub-exponential variable and compare with Chernoff bounds for a sum of 100 terms
Simulate sparse regression with n = 100 and p = 500, run the lasso over a lambda grid and plot the support recovery rate
Generate sample covariance matrices for p/n = 0.5 and plot the eigenvalue histogram against the Marchenko-Pastur density

schedule.title: Lower bounds, testing and phase transitions
schedule.exercise: Derive a minimax lower bound for estimating a sparse normal mean by a two-point argument, and simulate when variable selection with knockoffs controls false discoveries.

tasks.title: Compute the Le Cam two-point bound for estimating a normal mean from n observations and compare with the risk of the sample mean
Run a knockoff-style variable selection on simulated data with 200 predictors and measure the false discovery proportion against its target
Simulate the success probability of sparse recovery over a grid of sample size and sparsity and plot the phase transition curve

schedule.title: Empirical distributions and rank tests
schedule.exercise: Use the empirical distribution and the DKW inequality to build a confidence band, then compare the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with the t-test on heavy-tailed data and tune a kernel density bandwidth.

tasks.title: Plot an empirical distribution function for 30 observations with a DKW confidence band and apply the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against a fitted normal
Compare the power of the t-test and the Wilcoxon test for a location shift under normal and heavy-tailed data over 5000 simulations
Estimate a density with a Gaussian kernel, choose the bandwidth by cross-validation and compare with the rule-of-thumb bandwidth on mixture data

schedule.title: Smoothing, permutation and conformal inference
schedule.exercise: Fit a local polynomial regression to a noisy dataset, relate the bandwidth to the bias-variance trade-off and the convergence rate, and build a conformal prediction interval with guaranteed coverage.

tasks.title: Fit local linear regressions with five bandwidths and plot bias, variance and mean squared error against bandwidth on simulated data
Run a permutation test for a difference in means with 10000 shuffles and compare its p-value with the exact and the t-test values
Build split conformal intervals for a regression model and check that 90 percent coverage holds across 1000 repeated splits

schedule.title: Simulation study, proof writing and project
schedule.exercise: Present a project in which you derive an estimator, prove consistency and asymptotic normality, and report a Monte Carlo study of its finite-sample bias, variance and coverage.

tasks.title: Design a Monte Carlo study comparing three estimators over four sample sizes with 5000 replications and report bias, variance and Monte Carlo error
Derive the asymptotic variance of your project estimator and plot it beside the simulated variance across sample sizes
Reproduce one theorem from a statistical-theory paper by simulation, stating its assumptions and one case where they fail
